big_idea: Canadian BILLS: $5, $10, $20. Each has a different COLOUR and PERSON.
learning_intention: We are learning to identify bills up to $20.
student_learning_goal: I can identify bills up to $20.
success_criteria: I can SAY each bill's value.
I can MATCH bill to colour.
I can SORT bills by value.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Penny + Coin Cassie — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Coin Cassie: Friends — meet Cassie the Cashier! Today we look at PAPER MONEY — Canadian BILLS! Penny opens: 'NUMBER says VALUE. Read the WHOLE number!' (Class echoes.)
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Coin Cassie the Cashier puppet. 'Shoppers — yesterday we did COINS. Today we do BILLS!'

Define. 'BILL = paper money. Different from coins. Each bill has a COLOUR and a PERSON.'

Reveal each bill:

$5 BILL: BLUE colour. WILFRID LAURIER on front. '$5 is a fiver!'
$10 BILL: PURPLE colour. JOHN A. MACDONALD on front. '$10 is a tenner!'
$20 BILL: GREEN colour. QUEEN ELIZABETH II on front. '$20 is a twenty!'

'Cassie says — Canadian bills are PLASTIC! They feel like paper but they're polymer. CLEAR window with maple leaf!'

Demo. 'I'll hold up a bill. You name it!' Hold blue. Class: '$5!' Hold purple. Class: '$10!' Hold green. Class: '$20!'

'Cassie says — colour first, value second!'

Now show bills with coins. '1 toonie = $2. 1 fiver = $5. 1 toonie + 1 fiver = $7!'

'Cassie says — bills are BIGGER VALUES than coins!'

Now each pair gets the Bill Cards (15 bills — 5 each of $5, $10, $20). They sort by value.

'Cassie says — match colour to value!'

steps.instruction: VALUE-FIRST INTRODUCTION: Penny holds up $5. Class reads the WHOLE numeral aloud — 'FIVE dollars'. Same for $10 and $20. No size-based discussion until value is named.
steps.teacher_prompt: Penny: 'The NUMBER says the value. Read the whole number, every time.'

steps.instruction: COMPOSITION: Pairs build $10 two ways using bills only (one $10 OR two $5s). Then build $20 multiple ways (one $20, two $10s, four $5s). Class compares: 'same VALUE, different bills.'
INVENT-AND-COMPARE: Pairs invent a way to make $15 OR $20 using bills only — no constraints. Two pairs share methods side-by-side; class debates which is faster to count and which is harder to make.
steps.teacher_prompt: Penny: 'Different bills, same value. The math doesn't care HOW you build it — it cares about the TOTAL.'

steps.instruction: MISCONCEPTION CHECK: Penny shows $5 next to $20 and asks 'which is more?' Children must read whole numerals before answering. Front-digit and size-based errors are surfaced and named.
steps.teacher_prompt: Penny: 'NUMBER, not size. NUMBER, not the front digit. The WHOLE number says the value.'

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the bills tracker. Note misconceptions for tomorrow's compare-values lesson.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Five signals: names; values; sorts; matches colour; consistency.

discussion_prompts: Penny's preview: tomorrow we COMPARE values across coins AND bills (Lesson 4 — F1.1). What did today teach us about reading the value first, before deciding 'more' or 'less'?
consolidation.exit_routine: Penny's refrain — class chants 3x: 'COUNT the VALUE, not the bills!' Each child reads ONE bill aloud (full numeral) and names its value in dollars.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child says $5 > $20 — repairing the front-digit / size-based bill misreading
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On bills, the dominant Grade-1 F1.1 misconception is the FRONT-DIGIT error — child reads $20 as 'two dollars' because they latch onto the leading digit, OR claims $5 > $20 because '5 > 2'. The size-based variant: child says 'the BIGGER bill is worth more' and uses physical size as the cue (some children believe a $5 bill is worth more than $20 because $5 bills 'feel thicker'). Both are well-documented in early-numeracy research (Mix, Sandhofer & Baroody on numeral reading; Resnick on place-value misreading).

Today's task pivots the lesson from colour/recognition (Lesson 1-2 scope) to VALUE as the math object, with colour as a SECONDARY cue. Tomorrow we compare values across denominations (Lesson 4); without today's value-anchoring, that comparison has no foothold.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair has $5, $10, $20 paper bills (or printable replicas). Penny asks 'which has the highest value?' Child confidently picks $5.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. Read the WHOLE numeral aloud — not just the front digit: 'TWENTY dollars. Not two — TWENTY.' Hold up your hand and count: 'one — two — three... — TWENTY fingers and toes. That's how many loonies are in a twenty.'

If child uses size: lay all three bills end-to-end. 'Size doesn't say value. The NUMBER says value. What number do you see on this one?' Child reads. 'Twenty. So this bill is worth ___?' 'Twenty.'

Build composition: 'Show me $10 with this $10 bill. Now show me another way — two $5s.' Child swaps. 'Same value, different ways!'

Penny says — 'COUNT the VALUE, not the bills.' Repeat 3x.

Long-term recovery: every bill is read aloud as a full number before anyone moves it on the tray.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) 'The $5 is biggest because 5 is bigger than 2.'
(Mid) Reads $20 correctly after teacher prompt; needs reminder.
(Strong) Reads each bill as full number; orders correctly.
(Stretched) Builds same value two ways ($10 = one $10 or two $5s).
common_misconceptions: Front-digit reading: $20 = 'two dollars'. (Repair: read whole numeral.)
Size-based value: bigger physical bill = higher value. (Repair: number says value, not size.)
Colour-only recognition: name without value. (Repair: pin value to name.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — digit-based ($5 > $20 because '5 > 2'): drill reading the WHOLE numeral aloud — 'TWENTY, not two.' Use a chart with '20' broken into '2|0' showing the 0 makes it ten times bigger.
DIAGNOSTIC B — size-based ('bigger bill = more value'): lay bills end-to-end, say 'size doesn't say value, the NUMBER does.' Cover the bill except the numeral; child reads value.
DIAGNOSTIC C — names but stalls on value: build composition — 'show me $10 two ways' (one $10, two $5s). Same value, different physical look.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Anchor VALUE reading on bills; practise composition; surface front-digit misconception via transfer probe.

parts_outline.task: Read whole numeral; write value of each bill.
Build $10 two different ways using bills.
